:::{#def-invertible-matrix}
#### Invertible matrix (non-singular matrix)

A $p \times p$ matrix $\matr{A}$ is **invertible**
(or **non-singular**)
if some $p \times p$ matrix $\matr{B}$ satisfies

$$\matr{A}\matr{B} = \matr{B}\matr{A} = \matr{I}_p,$$

where $\matr{I}_p$ is the identity matrix (@def-identity-matrix).
A square matrix that is not invertible is **singular**.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-invertible-matrix}
#### An invertible matrix and a singular one

The matrix
$\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
is invertible, with
$\matr{A}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$:
multiplying out gives
$\matr{A}\matr{A}^{-1} = \matr{A}^{-1}\matr{A} = \matr{I}_2$.

The matrix
$\matr{M} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
is singular:
for any $2 \times 2$ matrix $\matr{C}$,
the two rows of $\matr{M}\matr{C}$ are equal,
so $\matr{M}\matr{C}$ can never be $\matr{I}_2$,
whose two rows differ.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-invertible-inverse}
#### Invertible matrices and inverses

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ matrix,
and suppose that two $p \times p$ matrices $\matr{B}$ and $\matr{C}$
satisfy
$\matr{A}\matr{B} = \matr{B}\matr{A} = \matr{I}_p$
and
$\matr{A}\matr{C} = \matr{C}\matr{A} = \matr{I}_p$.
Then

$$
\ba
\matr{B}
&= \matr{B}\,\matr{I}_p
&& \text{(identity matrix)}
\\
&= \matr{B}(\matr{A}\matr{C})
&& \text{(} \matr{A}\matr{C} = \matr{I}_p \text{)}
\\
&= (\matr{B}\matr{A})\matr{C}
&& \text{(matrix multiplication is associative)}
\\
&= \matr{I}_p\,\matr{C}
&& \text{(} \matr{B}\matr{A} = \matr{I}_p \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{C}
&& \text{(identity matrix)}
\ea
$$

The steps use @thm-matmul-assoc and @thm-identity.
Since $\matr{B} = \matr{C}$,
at most one matrix satisfies these equations,
which is the uniqueness that @def-matrix-inverse asserts.
When $\matr{A}$ is invertible,
the matrix $\matr{B}$ in @def-invertible-matrix
is therefore the inverse $\matr{A}^{-1}$ of $\matr{A}$,
and $\matr{A}$ is invertible exactly when it has an inverse.
For example,
for $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
in @exm-invertible-matrix,
$\begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
is the only $2 \times 2$ matrix $\matr{B}$
with $\matr{A}\matr{B} = \matr{B}\matr{A} = \matr{I}_2$,
so it is $\matr{A}^{-1}$.

:::
